Welcome to Day 2 of Health Insurance Subrogation Training. Yesterday we built the foundation. Today we look at the players behind every health insurance lien: the providers who treat our clients, the health insurance companies that pay the bills, and the subrogation companies that come back to collect from the settlement. By the end of today you should be able to look at a file and say who paid, who is asking to be repaid, and who you need to call.

Here is our road map for today. We start with health plan providers, meaning the doctors and hospitals who treat our clients. Then we cover health insurances and the different types of coverage. Next we look at in-network and out-of-network providers, because that affects what gets billed and paid. Finally we spend real time on subrogation companies, the outside vendors who usually send us the lien letters. Keep these four groups in mind as we go.

Let's start with the health insurance company. Its job is to provide coverage for medical expenses. After an accident it often steps in and pays the medical bills first. But if a third party is liable for the injury, the insurer may later seek subrogation to recover what it paid. That is exactly why health insurance shows up on our closing files. When you see that the health plan paid bills, assume a reimbursement claim may follow and plan for it.

Health providers are the hospitals, doctors, clinics and other medical professionals who actually treat our clients. They bill either the patient or the patient's insurance company for the services they render. Those charges can then be included in the injury claim after an accident. For you, providers matter in two ways. Their bills are part of the damages, and if their bills were paid by health insurance, that payment is what the insurer will later try to recover.

In-network providers have agreements with insurance companies to offer their services at reduced rates. Because of those agreements, the plan typically covers a higher percentage of the cost. When you review a file, knowing whether treatment was in network helps you understand why the amount the plan paid is lower than the provider's full charge. It also tells you that the provider has a contract with the plan, which affects how the bill was handled.

Out-of-network providers are the opposite. They have no contract with the client's particular insurance plan. Coverage for their services is generally less favorable, which means higher out-of-pocket costs for the patient. On an injury file, that often means a larger unpaid balance sitting with the provider, even when insurance paid part of the bill. Keep that in mind when you are gathering balances before settlement, because the client may owe more here than they realize.

Here is how an out-of-network bill moves. The provider submits the bill to the patient's health insurance. The insurer processes it and typically reimburses at a lower rate than it would pay an in-network provider. The patient may then receive a balance bill for the difference between what insurance paid and what the provider charged. So on one treatment you can have two claims against the settlement: the insurer's lien for what it paid, and the provider's balance.

Subrogation companies act on behalf of insurance providers. Their job is to recover the expenses the insurer covered for the insured's medical treatment. They pursue claims against the party responsible for the incident, or that party's insurance company, to reclaim those costs. On our side of the table, this is usually who sends the lien letter and who we negotiate with, so learn the names. We will go through the common companies later today.

Now let's connect the three players. First, the healthcare provider bills the health insurance company for treatment after the accident. Second, the health insurance company covers those expenses and may work with a subrogation company to recover the costs from a liable third party. Third, the subrogation company places a lien on any settlement so the insurer is reimbursed. When you open a file, try to name all three: who treated, who paid, and who is collecting.

This is why the relationship matters to us. In personal injury claims, subrogation often comes into play because health insurers seek reimbursement from settlements or judgments. At the same time, the goal is that the injured party is not left overburdened with unpaid medical bills. As Closing Specialists we sit right in the middle of that balance. We make sure valid claims are handled, and we work to protect the client's recovery.

Here is the whole story in plain words, told from the client's side. After a car accident, health insurance covers the medical costs. If another party is at fault, the insurer seeks reimbursement through subrogation, recovering from the at-fault party or their insurance. When the injury claim settles, the recovery first repays the health insurer before the client receives the remaining funds. This is a good way to explain liens to a client who asks why they are not getting the full settlement.

This is the workflow in three steps. There is a car accident. Health insurance pays, which the slide calls health insurance compensation. Then subrogation follows, where the plan seeks to be reimbursed. Notice the order: the lien is resolved after the case pays out, but our work on it should start long before. If we only discover the health plan at settlement, we lose time. Ask yourself: at which step should a Closing Specialist first think about the health insurance lien?

Now we move into health insurances: the main types of coverage, the government programs, the major companies, and a few key terms. As we go, think about how each type of coverage might show up on a closing file, and what questions you would ask a client to identify it early. In the United States, health insurance is a critical part of the healthcare system. It provides coverage for medical expenses and helps people get access to the services they need. For our clients, it is often the first source that pays for treatment after an accident. That is good for the client in the moment, but it also means the plan may come back later and ask to be repaid from the settlement. Next we will look at the types of coverage.

The first type is employer-sponsored insurance. It is provided by employers as a benefit to employees and often covers the employee and their family, with the employer paying a portion of the premium. This is one of the most common types you will see on injury files. When a client says their insurance is through work, write that down right away, because the kind of employer plan can affect the reimbursement rules that apply.

The second type is individual and family plans. These are purchased directly by individuals or families, either through the Health Insurance Marketplace or from private insurers. They are often subsidized based on income. When you collect insurance information, ask the client whether they bought the plan themselves or got it through a job, because that tells you which category you are dealing with and who to contact about a possible lien.

Here are the government programs. Medicare is the federal program for people sixty-five and older and some younger people with disabilities. Medicaid is a joint federal and state program for low-income individuals and families. CHIP, the Children's Health Insurance Program, covers children in low-income families who do not qualify for Medicaid but still need affordable coverage. A common mistake is mixing up Medicare and Medicaid when talking to clients, so be careful with those two names.

Short-term health insurance is a temporary plan that provides coverage for a limited duration. These plans are typically less comprehensive and less expensive than standard plans. On a file, that means you should check the coverage dates against the date of the accident and the dates of treatment. A client may have had coverage for some of their care but not all of it, which changes what was paid and by whom.

Catastrophic plans are low-premium, high-deductible plans. They are designed for young and healthy individuals who want protection against major health events. Because the deductible is high, the client may have paid a lot out of pocket before the plan paid anything. So when you review what the plan paid, do not be surprised if much of the smaller treatment shows as the client's responsibility rather than the insurer's.

Now the government-administered plans, starting with Medicare. It is administered by the federal government through the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, known as CMS. It covers individuals aged sixty-five and older, younger people with disabilities, and individuals with end stage renal disease. You will hear CMS a lot on Medicare files. If a client fits any of these groups, ask about Medicare early, because government liens are never something we can ignore.

Medicaid is managed jointly by the federal and state governments. It supports low-income individuals and families, including pregnant women, children, the elderly and people with disabilities. The key point for us is the last line: eligibility criteria and benefits can differ across states. So a Medicaid file in one state may not work like a Medicaid file in another. Always confirm which state's program paid before you assume anything about the process.

TRICARE is the military health program. It is administered by the Department of Defense, and it serves active-duty service members, retired military personnel and their families. If a client or a family member is in the military or retired from it, ask whether TRICARE paid for any treatment. It is easy to miss if you only ask about a regular health insurance card, so make it part of your intake questions.

ERISA stands for the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974. It is a federal law that sets minimum standards for pension and health plans in private industry to protect participants. It regulates retirement and health benefits provided by employers, and it is overseen by federal agencies such as the Department of Labor, the Internal Revenue Service and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation. When a lien letter mentions ERISA, flag it, because it tells you the plan is employer-provided.

Now some major health insurance companies in the US. UnitedHealthcare is one of the largest providers, offering a wide range of plans, including employer-sponsored, individual and Medicare plans. Because it offers so many types, the name on the card does not tell you the whole story. Always find out which kind of plan the client has, since an employer plan and a Medicare plan from the same company can be handled very differently.

Anthem operates under various names across the country and provides individual, employer and Medicare plans. The point to remember is the various names. A client may describe their insurance with a different brand name than the one on a lien letter, and it can still be the same company. When names do not match, confirm before you assume it is a separate lien or a mistake.

Cigna offers health insurance for individuals, families and employers, along with Medicare and international coverage. As with the other large carriers, the company name alone does not tell you which rules apply. Note the plan type from the card or from the client, and keep it in the file, so whoever picks up the lien later knows exactly what kind of coverage paid the bills.

Humana provides individual, family and Medicare plans, with a focus on integrated care. You will often see Humana on files for older clients because of its Medicare plans. When you see the name, ask whether the client's coverage is a Medicare plan, since that changes who you deal with and how the reimbursement is handled. Write the answer in the file so the team does not have to ask twice.

Blue Cross Blue Shield, or BCBS, is described here as a federation of thirty-six independent companies providing coverage in different regions under the BCBS brand. The practical lesson is that BCBS is not one company. A client's Blue Cross plan in one state is run by a different company than in another state. Always note which regional BCBS company paid, because that is who you will be dealing with on the lien.

Healthcare.gov is the federal website where individuals and families can shop for and enroll in health insurance plans, particularly when they do not have coverage through an employer. State-specific marketplaces also exist. If a client says they bought their plan online or through the marketplace, you know you are dealing with an individual or family plan, not an employer plan. That helps you sort out what kind of coverage paid.

Two terms you must know. Premiums are the monthly cost of the insurance. Deductibles are the amount the person pays out of pocket before insurance starts covering costs. Why does this matter to us? Because what the client paid toward a deductible is money the insurer did not pay. So the insurer's lien should only reflect what the insurer actually paid, not the client's own out-of-pocket share.

The second consideration is coverage and networks. A plan should cover the necessary services and have a network of healthcare providers that meets the person's needs. This ties back to what we covered on in-network and out-of-network providers. When a client treated outside their network, expect lower plan payments and possibly a balance bill from the provider, both of which you will need to account for at closing.

Now the third player: subrogation companies. We will cover their role, how the process works, who the key players are, and the common names you will see on lien letters. These are the companies you will talk to most often when resolving health insurance liens, so this part is very practical. Subrogation companies play a big part in managing and controlling insurance costs. By recovering funds, they help lower premiums and reduce the financial impact on insurers and policyholders. Their work also makes sure the responsible parties are held financially accountable for the damages or injuries they cause. Understanding their motive helps you negotiate: they are measured on what they recover, so come prepared with documents and clear numbers.

The first role is recovering costs. After an insurance company pays out for a claim, such as medical expenses or property damage, the subrogation company works to recover those costs from the responsible party or their insurance. On our files, the recovery usually comes from the client's settlement. So when a subrogation company contacts the firm, it is trying to get back what the plan already paid.

The second role is handling liens. Subrogation companies often place a lien on any settlement or judgment the injured party receives. The purpose is to make sure the insurance company is reimbursed before any remaining funds go to the claimant. This is why we cannot disburse to the client until known liens are resolved. Missing a lien can leave the client, and the firm, facing a claim after the money is gone.

The third role is negotiation. Subrogation companies negotiate with the at-fault party's insurer to recover the amount the original insurer paid, including any legal fees associated with the recovery process. When the client has a lawyer, the negotiation often happens with us instead. Be ready with the settlement amount, the itemized payments, and the reasons a reduction is fair.

The fourth role is legal coordination. Subrogation companies coordinate with legal teams to make sure subrogation claims are properly filed and that recovery efforts comply with the relevant laws and regulations. For us, that means our correspondence should be professional, accurate and in writing. Keep copies of everything you send and receive, because the lien file may be reviewed by lawyers on both sides.

Now how the process works, step by step. Step one is the insurance payment. An insurance company pays for covered expenses, such as medical costs or property repairs, after a claim is filed. On our files, this is the health plan paying the client's treatment bills. Everything that follows depends on this payment, so the first thing we always want is an itemized list of what the plan actually paid.

Step two is the subrogation process. The insurance company's subrogation department identifies whether another party is liable. Then the subrogation company is given the task of recovering the paid amount from the responsible party or their insurer. This is often when the firm receives its first letter or questionnaire from the subrogation company. Respond promptly and log it, because that letter opens the lien file.

Step three is claim recovery. The subrogation company pursues the claim, which may involve negotiation or litigation, to recover the funds. In our world, this is usually a negotiation with the firm once the injury case settles. Your preparation makes the difference here. A clean, documented file gives the firm a better chance of a fair result for the client.

Step four is settlement or judgment. Once recovery is achieved, the funds are used to reimburse the original insurer, so it is compensated for the amount it initially paid out. For the Closing Specialist, this means paying the agreed lien amount from the settlement and getting written confirmation that the lien is resolved. Do not close the file without that confirmation.

Now the key players in subrogation. First, insurance companies themselves. Many large insurers have their own subrogation departments or teams. So sometimes the lien letter really does come straight from the carrier. When that happens, you deal with the carrier's subrogation team directly, and you still need the same things: the itemized payments, a reference number, and the person handling the file.

Second, specialized subrogation firms. These companies focus only on subrogation, often working for multiple insurers to recover funds. This is why the same vendor name can appear on files with very different health plans. Get to know the common vendors and how they like to receive requests, because you will see them again and again.

Third, law firms. Some law firms have expertise in subrogation and handle the legal side of recovering funds for insurers. When a lien is handled by a law firm on the insurer's side, our correspondence becomes lawyer to lawyer in tone. Keep it accurate and professional, and loop in the attorney on our file when the other side raises legal arguments.

This slide sums up why so many health insurers outsource. By using a subrogation company, health insurance companies can manage their financial recoveries effectively and make sure responsible parties are held accountable for their liabilities. For us, the takeaway is simple. The company you negotiate with is often not the insurer on the client's card. Always identify who is actually handling the recovery before you send anything.

Here is who actually handles the recovery, in three steps. The health insurance pays the hospital expenses. The health insurer then engages a subrogation company to reclaim those expenses. The subrogation company goes after the at-fault insurance or the law firm that resolved the case. So the name on the lien letter is often a vendor, not the carrier. When the client is represented, that vendor works with us.

Now the most common subrogation companies in the US, the names you will see on lien letters. The Rawlings Group specializes in healthcare subrogation and works with health plans to recover costs. When a Rawlings letter arrives, treat it as the health plan's lien, log the reference number, and request an itemized list of payments so you can check every charge against the accident.

Optum provides subrogation services, particularly in healthcare and workers' compensation. You will see the Optum name often, and as the next slides show, several other vendor names are now part of the Optum group. That is why a single client file can sometimes involve correspondence under more than one name that leads back to the same organization.

Equian is noted here as now part of Optum. It focuses on cost containment solutions, including subrogation. If you see Equian on older correspondence and Optum on newer letters, do not assume there are two separate liens. Confirm with the vendor whether it is the same claim before you add anything to the net sheet.

Trover Solutions is described as a leading subrogation provider, particularly in healthcare recovery. Like the other vendors, it works on behalf of health plans. When a Trover letter comes in, the steps are the same: confirm which health plan it represents, get the reference number, and ask for the itemized payments.

Conduent offers subrogation services across multiple industries, including healthcare and property and casualty insurance. Because it works in more than one line, read its letters carefully to see exactly which payments and which plan the claim covers. Do not assume it is a health insurance lien until the letter or a phone call confirms it.

Gould and Lamb specializes in subrogation, with a focus on Medicare Secondary Payer compliance. That phrase tells you it deals with Medicare-related issues. When you see this name on a file, treat it with the same care as any government-related lien, and make sure the right person on the team is aware of it before settlement funds move.

Ingenix Subrogation Services is listed as part of the Optum group, focusing on healthcare cost recovery. Again, notice how many of these names lead back to Optum. The lesson across all of these vendors is the same: know who you are dealing with, keep their reference numbers, and confirm the plan they represent.

So how do you find out which subrogation company manages the lien for a particular health plan? You contact the provider, meaning the health insurance company, and ask for the information. Have the client's details ready when you call, and write down who you spoke with, the vendor name, and any reference number they give you. Ask yourself: what would you want written in the file before you hang up?

Thank you, that wraps up Day 2. Today we covered the providers, the types of health insurance, in- and out-of-network billing, and the subrogation companies that collect on the plans' behalf. Before next session, review the common vendor names so you recognize them on a lien letter.
